books.section: Topic 3.10 Shaping the New Republic, F. Policy Debates in the New Nation

primary_sources: Alexander Hamilton, Report on Public Credit (January 1790)
Thomas Jefferson, Opinion on the Constitutionality of a National Bank (February 1791)
Alexander Hamilton, Opinion on the Constitutionality of a National Bank (February 1791)

source: original; documents viewed before writing — all pre-1930 public-domain sources.
prompt: Evaluate the extent to which debates over Alexander Hamilton’s financial program led to the formation of the first political parties in the United States in the period 1789–1800.

documents.title: Alexander Hamilton, Report on Public Credit
documents.source: Alexander Hamilton, Report on Public Credit, January 1790. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Hamilton’s own plan for the nation’s debts, showing what he wanted the government to do.
documents.text: “A national debt, if it is not excessive, will be to us a national blessing.” Paraphrase: Hamilton proposed that the federal government pay the national debt at full value and take over the states’ war debts, funding both by selling government bonds.

documents.title: Thomas Jefferson, Opinion on the Constitutionality of a National Bank
documents.source: Thomas Jefferson, Opinion on the Constitutionality of a National Bank, February 15, 1791. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Jefferson’s objection to the bank, showing the strict reading of the Constitution behind the opposition.
documents.text: “To take a single step beyond the boundaries thus specially drawn around the powers of Congress, is to take possession of a boundless field of power, no longer susceptible of any definition.”

documents.title: Alexander Hamilton, Opinion on the Constitutionality of a National Bank
documents.source: Paraphrased from Alexander Hamilton, Opinion on the Constitutionality of a National Bank, February 23, 1791. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Hamilton’s answer to Jefferson, showing the broad reading of the Constitution behind the Federalists.
documents.text: Paraphrase: Hamilton argued that the necessary and proper clause lets Congress choose the means to carry out its listed powers, such as borrowing money and collecting taxes, and that a national bank was such a means.

documents.title: George Washington, Farewell Address
documents.source: George Washington, Farewell Address, published September 19, 1796. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Washington’s warning as he left office, showing how far party feeling had already grown.
documents.text: “Let me now take a more comprehensive view, and warn you in the most solemn manner against the baneful effects of the spirit of party generally.” Washington added that party spirit “serves always to distract the public councils and enfeeble the public administration.”

documents.title: The Sedition Act
documents.source: Paraphrased from the Sedition Act, July 14, 1798. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: A Federalist law of 1798, showing how the party fight reached into the law itself.
documents.text: Paraphrase: The act made it a crime to write, print, or publish false, scandalous, and malicious writings against the government of the United States, either house of Congress, or the president, with intent to defame them or bring them into contempt.

documents.title: James Madison, Virginia Resolution
documents.source: James Madison, Virginia Resolution, December 24, 1798. Public domain.
documents.sourcing: Madison’s answer to the Sedition Act, showing the opposition claiming a state check on federal power.
documents.text: “In case of a deliberate, palpable, and dangerous exercise of other powers, not granted by the said compact, the states who are parties thereto, have the right, and are in duty bound, to interpose for arresting the progress of the evil.”

documents.title: Electoral Votes for President, Election of 1800
documents.source: Electoral vote totals from the National Archives, 1800 Electoral College Results. Public record.
documents.sourcing: The counted votes of the election of 1800, showing the parties lined up behind rival candidates.
documents.text: Thomas Jefferson (Democratic-Republican), 73 electoral votes; Aaron Burr (Democratic-Republican), 73; John Adams (Federalist), 65; Charles Cotesworth Pinckney (Federalist), 64; John Jay (Federalist), 1. Total 138 electors; 70 votes needed to win. The tie between Jefferson and Burr sent the election to the House of Representatives, which chose Jefferson on the 36th ballot in February 1801.

rubric.criterion: Thesis: earns the point for a historically defensible claim that answers the prompt, stating the extent to which debates over Hamilton’s financial program led to the formation of the first political parties, with a clear line of reasoning.
rubric.notEarned: Restating the prompt with no claim about the extent does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Contextualization: earns the point for describing a broader historical context relevant to the prompt, such as the new Constitution putting the government into practice, the weight of the war debts, or the fear of distant authority after British rule.
rubric.notEarned: A sentence of background with no link to the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (first point): earns the point for describing the content of at least three documents relevant to the argument about Hamilton’s program and the rise of parties.
rubric.notEarned: Quoting documents without describing what they show does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence from documents (second point): earns the point for using the content of at least six documents to support the argument, including documents from both sides of the debate over Hamilton’s program.
rubric.notEarned: Using fewer than six documents, or using six without tying them to the argument, does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Evidence beyond the documents: earns the point for describing a specific relevant example not in the documents, such as the Whiskey Rebellion of 1794, the debate over Jay’s Treaty, the XYZ Affair and the Quasi-War, or the Residence Act bargain over the capital.
rubric.notEarned: A vague reference to outside knowledge with no specific example does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Sourcing: earns the point for explaining how the audience, purpose, historical situation, or point of view of at least two documents shapes the argument, such as Hamilton writing to persuade Congress to fund the debt, Jefferson writing to stop the bank, or Washington warning as he left office.
rubric.notEarned: Naming a document’s author without explaining how it shapes the argument does not earn the point.

rubric.criterion: Complexity: earns the point for a complex argument, such as qualifying the thesis by showing that the parties also grew from foreign policy and the Alien and Sedition Acts, not from the financial program alone, or that the parties organized opposition while claiming to oppose parties themselves.
rubric.notEarned: A second example with no qualification or weighing does not earn the point.

modelOutline:
Thesis: Debates over Hamilton’s financial program led to the first political parties to a great extent, because the program split the country over the size and purpose of the national government and gave each side a leader, a program, and a cause to organize around, though foreign policy and the Alien and Sedition Acts deepened the split.
Context: The Constitution was new in 1789, the government carried heavy war debts, and no one knew how strong the national government would be in practice, so Hamilton’s plans were the first test of what the Constitution allowed.
The program: Document 1 shows Hamilton calling a funded national debt a blessing and proposing to pay the debt at full value and take over the states’ debts, tying creditors to the national government.
The constitutional split: Document 2 shows Jefferson warning that stepping beyond Congress’s listed powers opens a boundless field of power, while Document 3 shows Hamilton answering with the necessary and proper clause, so the bank fight became a fight over strict and broad readings of the Constitution.
Parties in the open: Document 4 shows Washington warning against the spirit of party in 1796, proof that party feeling was already strong, and Document 7 shows the election of 1800 fought between two party tickets, Jefferson and Burr against Adams and Pinckney.
The fight turns bitter: Document 5 shows the Federalists making criticism of the government a crime, and Document 6 shows Madison answering that the states could interpose against unconstitutional laws, so the party fight reached the law and the states.
Beyond the documents: The Whiskey Rebellion of 1794 showed western farmers resisting Hamilton’s excise tax, and the fight over Jay’s Treaty split the country over Britain and France, giving the parties foreign causes as well as financial ones.
Complexity: The financial program started the parties, but it did not finish them, because the same men who warned against parties organized them, and the parties that formed over the bank were then driven apart further by war, neutrality, and the Sedition Act.
